title: Building & Breaking an MCP Permission Broker (Approval Is Not Human Presence)
thesis: When a coding agent runs as the same Unix user as its human, an Approve click is only input the agent may be able to produce, so sensitive capabilities need a separately protected proof of human presence that the agent cannot read, write, replay or route around. Even then, per-session grants are not isolation: the surrounding environment is part of the boundary.
summary: McMillin runs 20 to 30 coding-agent sessions at once on his personal workstation, some started by hand and some by cron jobs, and wanted only specific sessions to hold privileged capabilities such as Kubernetes access or a logged-in browser. His starting point was a kubeconfig file and a skill pointing at it, which, he says, any agent could discover. He built an MCP permission broker: each session gets an OAuth client identity held in memory, requests a named capability, and a human approves with a six-digit one-time code from a phone authenticator that never enters agent context. Grants name a session, a capability and an expiry, usually two hours, and can be revoked. He states the attacker position up front: the agent has his UID, admin group membership, broker-operator group membership, admin-socket access, a writable source checkout and a valid session, but no root and no passwordless sudo. He then walks three attack routes (steal or write the verifier state, replace policy or bypass enforcement, forge an approval), shows each is refused, and cites a historical evaluation of 15 defined checks. He then reports a twist: all checks were green while a database migration had broken the human approval path, locking him out. The talk closes with a live demo that a new terminal multiplexer, Rex, let one session drive another session's tab and borrow its browser grant, which he says erased the per-session guarantee. He offers a five-step repeatable boundary test and reference code.
argument: Hiding a credential file or leaving it out of a prompt is not an access-control boundary, because agents discover config files and skills and will use any access that makes the task easier.

If the agent shares the human's UID, an approval response is just agent-reachable input, so the broker must verify a separately protected factor (a TOTP code from an enrolled phone) rather than trust the answer, and must protect the verifier's seed, database, policy and socket as well as its API.

Three attack routes (state, routing, approval) all meet the same service-owned reference monitor, and each was tested and refused, with failure closed rather than falling back to a weaker local store.

Passing refusal tests and health checks does not show the system works: a migration broke the human approval path while every refusal check stayed green, so tests must cover success and upgrades from historical disk states as well as denial.

A one-time code proves a human was present, not that they understood or consented to the action, and per-session grants do not stop one session borrowing another's authority unless the sessions are actually isolated.
The environment is part of the boundary: installing a terminal multiplexer that lets sessions control each other's tabs defeated the broker's guarantees without any new grant being issued.

claims.claim: The speaker runs 20 to 30 concurrent coding-agent sessions on one workstation, started by him or by cron jobs, so per-session scoping of privileged capabilities matters.
A kubeconfig file plus a skill that points to it is discoverable by any agent on the machine, so omitting a credential from a prompt does not control access.
claims.evidence: His own prior setup; the slide states 'Not mentioning a credential is not an access-control boundary.'

claims.claim: An agent cannot approve its own permission request: an agent-authored elicitation response with action 'accept' and no factor is refused and leaves 0 active grants.
claims.evidence: Demo A on screen showing the broker refusing and the audit record; slide 04 gives the send, expect, verify steps.

claims.claim: From the agent's UID, reading the service-owned TOTP seed and opening the policy database for a direct grant write both fail with EACCES.
claims.evidence: Slide 06 shows the two denied operations; the speaker notes that if the agent UID equals the user UID the user must also be locked out of those files.

claims.claim: Replacing policy over the admin socket with an agent-authored file is refused ('--seed is not accepted over admin socket'), and pointing at a nonexistent admin socket is refused with no silent local-store fallback.
claims.evidence: Slide 07 shows the commands and refusal text; no live run of these two shown.

claims.claim: Forged approvals fail on both paths: the CLI refuses no code and a fabricated code, and an MCP elicitation with action accept plus a fabricated code returns presence_check_failed with no new grant.
A historical evaluation passed 15 of 15 defined checks (5 state, routing and provisioning, 8 capability checks, 2 postconditions) and 4 probe sessions ended with 0 active grants.
claims.evidence: Slide 09, labeled documented historical results; the slide adds that 15 checks are not 15 exploit techniques and the historical web UI was not live-tested.

claims.claim: The human approval path broke in production while all service-health and refusal checks stayed green: a migration advanced the version but the disk held an old permission_requests table missing trusted_* columns, producing HTTP 500 'no column named trusted_title'.
claims.evidence: His own incident, shown on slide 12 with the error text; he says he locked himself out a couple of times.

claims.claim: The broker's one-time code gives only evidence that some human said yes; it does not establish who holds the phone, informed consent, transaction signing or protection after the factor is compromised.
claims.evidence: Reasoning on slide 14, which lists what is enforced (single-use factor, 5 failures then 5-minute lockout, scope, expiry, revocation) against what is not established.

claims.claim: Installing the Rex terminal multiplexer let an agent in a session with no browser grant drive another tab that held a browser grant, so existing authority was borrowed without any new grant being issued.
claims.evidence: Live demo on a replayed run in which a session told to use the Rex browser tab handed the browser-agent MCP task to the authenticated session; slide 15 shows Session A, Rex control, Session B, browser.

claims.claim: The broker enforces different grants per session, but preventing borrowed authority additionally requires isolation; the same UID is not a sandbox.
claims.evidence: Slide 03 states the two properties separately.

claims.claim: Ambient credentials such as git or the GitHub CLI and AWS CLI are an unsolved gap in his setup; his interim fix is wrapper commands that check for an authorized session, and he may move agents to a separate OS user.
claims.evidence: His answer to an audience question; no results given.

frameworks.name: Attacker position versus protected state
frameworks.description: Define the boundary before testing. Attacker holds the human UID, admin and broker-operator groups, admin-socket access, a writable checkout and a valid session. Protected: service identity, deployed verifier and its state, the enrolled phone; admin-group membership is not unrestricted sudo.

frameworks.name: Three routes to unauthorized authority
frameworks.description: State (steal the factor, write a grant), routing (replace policy, bypass the monitor), approval (fake a decision, forge the factor). All three meet the same protected authority.

frameworks.name: Service-owned reference monitor
frameworks.description: MCP client elicitation response, CLI over a restricted admin socket and web UI approval form all feed one monitor that verifies the factor, calls _insert_grant, and records session plus capability plus expiry. Protected state is the policy DB, TOTP seed and audit trail.

frameworks.name: Claim versus proof
frameworks.description: An agent-controlled 'accept' is only a claim; a protected verifier checks the factor, not the answer. No valid factor means no grant.

frameworks.name: Repeatable boundary test
frameworks.description: Five steps: define the boundary, attack three routes, inspect authority (refusal reasons, grants, audit), prove both paths (human success, replay refusal, revocation, cleanup), test real upgrades from historical database shapes. Run only in an authorized environment with a harmless capability and retain evidence.

frameworks.name: Broker profiles
frameworks.description: Approval page offers agent-runner, coding, default (read-only TaskManager), personal-trusted (allow-all-minus-deny, marked fail-open), review, and ui-coding (adds browser-agent). Capability 'permission packs' such as browser access or agent-job access are requested per role for about two hours.

slide_only: Slide 02 title: 'Not mentioning a credential is not an access-control boundary.' The slide lists what the speaker needed: one session, one capability, bounded revocable authority.
Slide 03 footer: 'Same UID is not a sandbox. Cross-session control can borrow existing authority.'

Approval page shown in the demo lists profiles agent-runner, coding, default, personal-trusted (marked fail-open: allows everything not explicitly denied), review and ui-coding, and a warning that the client's display name ('Pi Coding Agent') is chosen by the client itself and is not verified. Callback was http://127.0.0.1:53787/callback.

Coding-profile policy on the approval page: an allow list of agents.get_*, agents.spawn_* and many nexus.* task, memory, wiki and milestone operations; deny list agents.admin_*, nexus.admin_* and nexus.delete_*; fail_open false; servers agents and nexus. Optional shared coding work period, 4h deadline preview.
Slide 06 note: if agent UID equals user UID, the user must be restricted from the seed file and the grant database.
Slide 07 refusal text: '--seed is not accepted over admin socket' and 'no silent local-store fallback'; takeaway 'The caller must not be routed through a weaker authority when checks fail.'

Slide 09 footnote: 15 checks are not 15 exploit techniques; dated sources and matrix are in appendix A1 to A3. Slide 10 footnote: web shares the implementation path, historical web UI not live-tested. Slide 16 points to appendix A4 for the full procedure and evidence checklist. The appendices were not shown.
Slide 11 'All green. Would you ship it?': service health green, refusal checks green, 'actually accessible' unknown.

Slide 13 Demo B steps: prepare sessions A and B asking to open example.com; review and approve A with a fresh code; immediately replay the code in B and inspect the already-used refusal; return to A for the result. Code never enters chat.

Slide 14: Not established: who holds the phone, informed consent, transaction signing, protection after factor compromise. 'Factor access is not informed consent. Session permissions are not same-UID sandboxing.'

Terminal frames: status bar shows model gpt-6.1-sol medium; the human-presence prompt reads 'Human-presence code (6 digits) (required) ... Each code works once.'; a replayed earlier run reports a page title '[un]prompted III - AI Security & Our New Overlords' for localhost:8000; the live run in view failed with ERR_SSL_PROTOCOL_ERROR on https://localhost:8000.
demos: Demo A: the Pi wrapper asks which broker profile to use; with the coding profile a human supplies a phone one-time code on the approval page and the agent gets access. Repeated without authenticating, the agent has no tool access and the broker returns the same error on deny.

Human path: the agent searches for a browser tool, finds none, calls permission_request_create for browser-agent; the human is prompted for a six-digit code outside agent context; after approval 63 broker tools appear and browser_agent_open_url is called. The live run failed with an SSL protocol error on https://localhost:8000 (a replayed earlier run succeeded and reported the page title).

Rex cross-tab demo: a session with no browser grant is told to use the Rex browser tab; it finds the other tab's capability through the rex skill and tries to drive it, borrowing the already-granted browser MCP access. The speaker concludes the grant boundary is defeated by the multiplexer.

offense: Agent reads or edits the verifier's on-disk TOTP seed or the SQLite grant database because it shares the human's UID.
Agent reloads the broker with its own policy file, or points the admin socket at a nonexistent path hoping for a fail-open local fallback.
Agent answers its own approval prompt: an MCP elicitation response with action accept, with the factor omitted or fabricated.
Agent discovers credential files and skills (a kubeconfig referenced in a skill) and uses them because they make the task easier.
Cross-session borrowing: a tool that lets one agent session drive another's terminal tab, as Rex did, lets an ungranted agent use an already-granted browser MCP session without any new grant.
Replaying a still-valid one-time code from a second session; the design target is a code that works once and expires.
defense: Run the verifier as a separate service identity and make the TOTP seed, policy database, deployed code and policy source unreadable and unwritable by the agent UID, including the human user when the UIDs match.
Verify a separately protected factor in the monitor and ignore the agent-supplied 'accept'; keep the code out of agent context entirely (browser page or extension prompt).
Fail closed: refuse reloads of policy over the admin socket and refuse silent fallback to a local store if the broker socket is missing.
Make every grant name a session, a capability and an expiry (about two hours), with revocation, and a single-use code with a 5-failure, 5-minute lockout.
Wrap ambient credential tools (gh, cloud CLIs) with checks for an authorized session, or run agents under a separate OS user.
Test the success path and real upgrades from historical disk states, and inspect final authority state and audit records, not only error messages.
Treat the environment as part of the boundary: disable or isolate cross-session control features and review any tool installed on agent hosts.
takeaways: On your own agent platform, let the agent answer its own approval request and check whether new authority appears.

On one operator's home-lab evidence, if agents share a UID with humans, stop treating UI approvals as a boundary; require a factor held by a verifier the agent UID cannot read or write, and prefer a separate agent user or sandbox.
On one incident's evidence, add success-path and upgrade-from-old-schema tests to security control suites. Then a broken human path is caught, not only a permissive one.
Inventory developer-host tooling (terminal multiplexers, IDE agents, session managers) for features that cross trust boundaries between agent sessions.
Be explicit about what a human-presence factor proves (presence) and does not (consent, comprehension), and design grants with narrow scope and short expiry accordingly.
limits: Controls are tailored to his home lab: the agent cannot get root and there is no passwordless sudo; other environments would need different guarantees.
Grants do not isolate sessions; if one session can affect or talk to another, the isolation breaks.
The one-time pad proves a human was present, not that they understood the action.
Ambient credentials (git, GitHub CLI, AWS CLI) remain unresolved; wrappers get in the way of human use.
The historical web UI was not live-tested, and 15 checks are not 15 exploit techniques.
critique: The attack results are a single-author, single-machine evaluation with no adversarial agent trial counts shown; '15 of 15' counts defined checks the author designed, which the slide itself says are not 15 techniques.

The attacks tested were file-permission and API-misuse attempts; no results were shown for a goal-directed agent searching for TOCTOU, process-level (ptrace, same-UID signals) or clipboard and screen-reading routes to the code, which same-UID separation does not obviously stop.
The talk's title claim is supported by reasoning and demonstrations, not by measured data.
The live demo of the human path failed on an SSL error, so the successful end-to-end result relied on an earlier recording shown in a replay frame.
qa: Q: How do you restrict agents' access to ambient credentials such as authenticated git, GitHub CLI or AWS CLI? A: Sandboxed agents would cover it but handicap him, so for now he wraps tools such as gh with overrides that check for an authorized session or an extra credential, which also gets in a human's way; he may move agents to a separate user and has to decide whether the box is agent-first or human-first.

Q: Do you use per-privilege-action profiles? A: Not per action, since he does not want to babysit; there is a standard coding profile (pull tasks, create PRs, merge after reviewer checks pass) plus permission packs such as browser access or agent-job access that he requests for two hours, RBAC style. He is working on just-in-time access for Kubernetes.

Q (session chair): If you only need to confirm a human is present, why not a simpler approve interface? A: He is considering a mobile app with push notifications for yes or no, building on a decision ping he already has for agents that need a human; the chair joked about the future keyboard having only an approve key, and he agreed it makes him the meat puppet of his agents.

key_frames.caption: Architecture: MCP client, CLI and web UI all feed one service-owned reference monitor (verify factor, _insert_grant, session plus capability plus expiry) guarding the policy DB, TOTP seed and audit trail.
Threat model: attacker holds the human UID, admin and operator groups, admin socket, writable checkout and valid session; separates per-session grants from isolation.
Historical evaluation results: 15 of 15 checks, 4 probe sessions with 0 active grants, with the caveat that 15 checks are not 15 techniques.
The migration incident: an old table lacking trusted_* columns broke the human approval path while all refusal checks passed.
Rex cross-tab bypass: Session A with no browser grant drives Session B's tab, borrowing existing authority.

signal.reason: The talk presents a threat model and test plan for coding agents that share the user's UID, shows two failures (passing tests with a broken human approval path, and an environment bypass), and rests on a single-user home-lab evaluation.

caveats: The video description says Dropbox; the title slide says The Browser Company and he says he left Dropbox about four months before, and this record uses the slide.
The captions say PI and cloud code; the slides and the speaker say the Pi coding agent and Claude Code, and this record uses those.

The speaker said the one-time code lives 30 seconds and the grant default is 2 hours; the slides say each code works once, with a 5-failure lockout and a 4-hour coding-profile deadline preview, and this record keeps both because the repo's exact lifetimes were not shown.
Appendix slides A1 to A4 are referenced but were not shown; the evaluation matrix and dated sources are not available from the video.
The replay of the earlier successful browser run is visible only in part, as terminal output; the page title text '[un]prompted III' is read from it as shown.
